name: Potong gigi tooth filing

card.summary: Potong gigi is the Balinese Hindu rite of filing the upper front teeth level, a coming-of-age ceremony that leaves an even, flattened smile line.
card.note: A religious rite performed by trained practitioners; filing removes enamel permanently.

quick.overview:
Potong gigi, meaning cut teeth, is a Balinese Hindu rite of passage in which the upper canine and front teeth are filed until even. The teeth are flattened, not sharpened, and the ceremony marks the passage into adulthood.

Its purpose is spiritual rather than cosmetic: Balinese tradition links the filed teeth to reducing negative emotions such as anger and jealousy. The outcome is nevertheless a visibly altered, even smile line, which is why it appears among body-modification topics in appearance communities.
quick.how: The ceremony is performed on teenagers, who dress in traditional clothing and are carried by parents so they do not touch the ground. A priest officiates and the filing is done by a specialist. Afterwards the young person is regarded as an adult, eligible for marriage.
quick.risks: Filing removes enamel, which does not grow back, so any change is permanent. Wikipedia's coverage of the Balinese rite does not address health effects; dental professionals generally describe enamel removal as carrying a risk of sensitivity and decay. It is a cultural practice, and outsiders should treat it as one.

lead: Potong gigi, literally cut teeth, is a Balinese rite in which a young person's upper teeth are filed to an even line [1]. Wikipedia describes the canine teeth as thought to represent negative emotions such as anger and jealousy, and the filing as a way to spiritually separate the person from animal instincts and ancestors [1].

The Balinese Hinduism article lists tooth filing (metatah) among rites of passage marking a change in spiritual and social status, with the six upper canine and front teeth filed after puberty and a high priest officiating [2]. After the ceremony the teenager is seen as an adult who may marry [1].
Tooth filing for beauty occurs in other cultures, such as the Herero, the Mentawai and Timor, but the Balinese practice is mainly spiritual, and the teeth are flattened rather than pointed [1].

chain: Upper canines and front teeth are filed level
angle.text: The rite changes the shape of the teeth to an even line, which in Balinese culture signals maturity and a refined, civilised state. Its motive is spiritual, though the altered smile is the visible result.

paras: The ceremony takes place after puberty. The participant wears traditional clothing and is carried so as not to touch the ground, which is meant to avoid evil forces; a modern version has teens wear socks [1].

The filing is tied to refraining from lust and evil impulses, and to separating the person from animalistic instincts [1]. It is one of the rites of passage of Balinese Hinduism, officiated by a high priest [2].
Other peoples, including the Herero, Mentawai and residents of Timor, file teeth for beauty. The Mentawai use no anaesthetic and bite wood during the procedure [1].
